newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak court opens way for presidential referendum.
newsitem.headline: Slovak court opens way for presidential referendum.

text.p: Slovakia's Constitutional Court opened the way on Wednesday for a referendum on direct presidential elections by rejecting a government motion to declare it illegal.

"The government motion has been rejected because the government is not legally charged to carry out the referendum," court spokeswoman Marianna Mochnacova said from the court's headquarters in Kosice, eastern Slovakia.
The parliamentary faction of Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar's Movement for a Democratic Slovakia (HZDS), the senior coalition partner, said it would abide by the court's decision.
"(The HZDS) will respect the ruling of the court," faction chairman Tibor Cabaj told the official TASR news agency.

The three-party ruling coalition last month suspended preparations for the referendum, due to be held on May 23-24 alongside another on whether Slovakia should join NATO, pending the court's decision.
Meciar's government wanted the court to declare the referendum unconstitutional in the hope of postponing or preventing it.

The referendum was seen as an attempt to prevent Meciar from assuming presidential powers when President Michal Kovac, an avowed political foe of the premier, steps down at the end of his term next March.
The vote on presidential elections was called after an opposition-initiated petition. Kovac and the parliamentary opposition have urged Slovaks to vote "yes" in both referendums.

The court later on Wednesday also ruled against a motion by Kovac that his constitutional rights had been violated when the referendum preparations were suspended on the grounds the motion had been lodged by an unauthorised person.
A spokesman for the interior ministry, charged with organising the plebiscite, said it would wait until it received the rulings officially before making any comment.
There was no immediate reaction from the president's office.

Under the present constitution, the president is elected by parliament, requiring a three-fifths majority. But in the present parliament neither the ruling coalition nor the opposition would be able to muster the necessary majority.
Presidential powers would then pass to the prime minister pending new parliamentary elections in the autumn of 1998.
The court said the ruling stipulated the Interior Ministry and the referendum commission had the duty to ensure the referendum was carried out.
"If the interior minister refuses to fulfill his duties he will be committing a felony," Ivan Simko, deputy chairman of the opposition Christian Democratic Movement, told TASR.
